solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Bitter speech from US attorney about island race

indicators.note: one thing placed about another wraps around it, so the attorney goes around the island

parts.note: a DA is a District Attorney, the American public prosecutor
I is the standard abbreviation for island on maps
a race or people sharing ancestry

explanation.surface: A prosecutor makes a bitter speech about an island people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Race' looks like a contest but means a people; the island letter sits between the two letters of the attorney.
explanation.definitionFit: A diatribe is a bitter, angry verbal attack, which is a speech full of venom.

clue.text: Talk about girl coming out at end of June

parts.note: a deb (debutante) is a young woman making her formal entry into society
taken as it stands

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only the tail of 'June' is used

parts.note: the final letter of the month

explanation.surface: Gossip about a young woman who made her society debut at the end of June.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coming out' is the old society sense: a debutante 'comes out' at her first ball, and the clue word 'at' is used literally.
explanation.definitionFit: To debate a subject is to discuss or argue over it, a verb synonym for talking it through.

clue.text: A deadly sin all right

parts.note: taken as it stands
greed (avarice) is one of the seven deadly sins

explanation.surface: Someone declares that one of the deadly sins is perfectly fine.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface seems to excuse a sin; really 'all right' is an exclamation of assent standing on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'Agreed!' and 'All right!' are interchangeable exclamations of consent in reply to a proposal.

clue.text: People on line for Belmont Park, perhaps

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece sitting on another is placed above it, so 'people' comes first

parts.note: a race is a people or ethnic group
a track is a line, as in a railway line

explanation.surface: A crowd queuing to get into Belmont Park.
explanation.walkthrough: Belmont Park is a horse-racing course in New York, home of the Belmont Stakes; 'perhaps' signals it is one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Belmont Park is a specific instance of a venue where horses compete, so it exemplifies the general term.

clue.text: Graduate in robe, fat scholar, ungainly

indicators.note: something ungainly is awkward and ill-arranged, so the letters before it are jumbled

parts.note: anagram fodder, 14 letters

explanation.surface: A clumsy, portly academic shuffles along in a graduation gown.
explanation.walkthrough: The graduation robe fits the surface neatly, which hides that 'robe' is just raw letters for the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone holding a BA degree has completed a university course, so is one kind of graduate.

clue.text: Foolish better, impulsive

parts.note: mad = crazy, foolish
to cap a story is to better or outdo it

explanation.surface: A reckless gambler placing silly, hasty bets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' reads as a noun, a person who bets; it is really the verb meaning to outdo.
explanation.definitionFit: A madcap scheme or person is reckless and acts on sudden whims without thought.

clue.text: Top celebrities included by journalists?

indicators.note: the answer is held within the letters of the following word

parts.note: the letters run across the middle of this word

explanation.surface: Famous people being featured in the press.
explanation.walkthrough: journ(ALIST)s: the question mark admits that celebrities really are 'included by journalists' in their stories.
explanation.definitionFit: The A-list is the group of most famous stars, those whose names are highest on invitation lists.

clue.text: Opening lines in court

parts.note: an opening is an opportunity, a chance
RY is the abbreviation for railway, i.e. lines

explanation.surface: A barrister's first words in a courtroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening lines' looks like one phrase for a speech's start; it splits into two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Chancery is the Chancery Division of England's High Court, historically the Lord Chancellor's court of equity.

clue.text: Priggish girl in pale yellow

parts.note: prim = stiffly proper, priggish
a girl's name

explanation.surface: A prudish young woman dressed in a pale yellow outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like it puts one piece inside another; here it only links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Primrose names a soft pale shade taken from the colour of the spring flower's petals.

clue.text: Propose father, male on mission, breaks into supply

parts.note: pop is an informal word for dad

indicators.note: to break into something is to force a way inside it, so the man on his mission goes inside the supply

parts.note: read as POTION, a dose supplied, sharing its first two letters with the father
he = a male person
a quest is a mission or search

explanation.surface: A man on a mission bursting into a stockroom.
explanation.walkthrough: The supply part is loose: the likeliest intent is a potion, a dose supplied, sharing its opening letters with the father, with the man on his mission inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To pop the question is the idiom for asking someone to marry you, i.e. making a marriage proposal.

clue.text: Penniless bachelor caught in Cairo, embarrassed

indicators.note: something caught in a place is trapped inside it, so the cricket letter goes inside the city

parts.note: B is the standard abbreviation for bachelor
c = caught in cricket scoring

indicators.note: an embarrassed person is thrown into confusion, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: anagram fodder once the extra letter is added

explanation.surface: A bachelor, broke and red-faced after being arrested in Egypt's capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Boracic is British rhyming slang: boracic lint = skint, i.e. broke. B is followed by a jumble of CAIRO with C inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Boracic is British slang for having no money, from rhyming slang on the word skint.

clue.text: Ring French friend about fake Japanese art

indicators.note: the ring and the friend together go around the word for fake

parts.note: O is ring-shaped
ami is French for friend
to rig is to fix or falsify, as with an election

explanation.surface: Phoning a French friend about a forgery of Japanese art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' tempts as a phone call; it is the ring-shaped letter, which teams up with the friend so the pair wraps around the fake.
explanation.definitionFit: Origami is the traditional Japanese craft of folding paper into decorative shapes such as cranes.

clue.text: Showing time for son in delightful message

indicators.note: one thing given for another replaces it, so time takes the place of son

parts.note: T is the standard abbreviation for time
S is the abbreviation for son in genealogies
sweet = charming, delightful

explanation.surface: A lovely note from a son showing he has time for his parents.
explanation.walkthrough: SWEET has its S swapped for T.
explanation.definitionFit: A tweet is a short post on the social network formerly called Twitter, a brief online message.

clue.text: Dash back across country in station wagon

indicators.note: stretching across something means lying either side of it, so the dash spans the country
going back means running the dash from right to left

parts.note: to race = to dash
a state is a nation or country

explanation.surface: Driving hurriedly back across the country in a family car.
explanation.walkthrough: ECAR splits around STATE. 'Station wagon' is the American name for what Britons call an estate car.
explanation.definitionFit: The British estate car and American station wagon are the same vehicle body with an extended rear load area.

clue.text: Retract what was said in quarrelsome conversation after European makes amends

indicators.note: the quarrel comes after the other pieces in the answer's order

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for European
to atone is to make amends
to have words with someone is to argue

explanation.surface: A European apologises by withdrawing remarks made during a heated row.
explanation.walkthrough: The order runs E, then ATONES, then WORDS, though the clue presents the quarrel first.
explanation.definitionFit: To eat one's words is the idiom for admitting a statement was wrong and withdrawing it.

clue.text: Pulling across lake in sport

indicators.note: stretching across something means lying either side of it, so the pulling spans the lake

parts.note: wresting = pulling or wrenching away
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A tug-of-war across a lake as a sporting contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulling' reads as the sport's action, but it is the word for wrenching that opens to take the lake.
explanation.definitionFit: Wrestling is a combat sport in which two opponents grapple to pin or throw each other.

clue.text: I'm dividing possessions for valuation

indicators.note: something dividing a whole splits it in two, so the 'I'm' sits in the middle of the possessions

parts.note: an estate is everything a person owns
taken as it stands

explanation.surface: An executor splitting up a dead person's belongings to value them.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures probate, where an estate really is divided and valued, so the wordplay hides in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: An estimate is an approximate judgement of worth or cost, which is what a valuation provides.

clue.text: A figure of speech to hamper translation

indicators.note: a translation turns words into a different form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: An idiom that is hard to render into another language.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a translator's complaint about idioms, which fits a metaphor perfectly.
explanation.definitionFit: A metaphor describes something as being something else, one of the classic rhetorical devices of language.

clue.text: Convey much significant information in address books

parts.note: to address an audience is to speak to it
volumes are books

explanation.surface: Contact details in an address book reveal a great deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Address books' reads as one object; it splits into a verb and a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that speaks volumes is highly revealing, telling a great deal without words.

clue.text: Meal's about over

parts.note: re = about, concerning
over = finished, past

explanation.surface: Dinner is nearly finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About over' reads as 'nearly done'; it is two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Repast is a formal or literary word for a meal, particularly one that is eaten at a table.

clue.text: On completion produces key

parts.note: on is the leg side in cricket
the end is the completion

explanation.surface: Finishing a job yields the vital element.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the on side, also called the leg side, is the half of the field behind the batsman's legs.
explanation.definitionFit: A map's legend is the panel explaining its symbols, also called the key.

clue.text: Rain's rare for resort, but overdue

indicators.note: resort read as re-sort means sorting over again, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: A holiday resort seldom sees rain, but the dry spell is late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' pretends to be a holiday town; it is split as re-sort.
explanation.definitionFit: Payments that are in arrears are late, owed but not yet paid by the due date.

clue.text: To get there some hire a charabanc

indicators.note: only some of the following letters are wanted, a run taken from within them

parts.note: the letters run across the three words

explanation.surface: Advice to rent a coach for the journey.
explanation.walkthrough: hi(RE A CH)arabanc. A charabanc is an old British word for a sightseeing coach.
explanation.definitionFit: To reach a place is to arrive at it, the same as managing to get there.

clue.text: Subject of article: Middle East

parts.note: the definite article
ME is the abbreviation for Middle East

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece whose topic is the Middle East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' suggests a newspaper piece; it is the grammatical article.
explanation.definitionFit: A theme is the main topic or idea running through a discussion or piece of writing.

clue.text: Really try in a bike racing event

parts.note: taken as it stands

indicators.note: the word for try goes inside the racing event

parts.note: the TT (Tourist Trophy) is the Isle of Man motorbike race
a judge tries or hears a case

explanation.surface: Urging a rider to make a real effort in a motorbike race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Try' reads as 'make an effort'; it is the legal sense, to hear a case in court.
explanation.definitionFit: At heart means fundamentally or in truth, the same sense as really or basically.

clue.text: Mimic one Italian introduced to pal

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: something introduced to another is put into it, so the Italian goes inside the pal

parts.note: a mate is a friend
It is the abbreviation for Italian

explanation.surface: An Italian impressionist being introduced to a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Introduced to' suggests a meeting; it puts the Italian inside the pal, with the one standing in front.
explanation.definitionFit: To imitate is to copy someone's behaviour or voice, exactly what a mimic does.

clue.text: Crude burrow close to shrubbery

parts.note: an earth is a fox's burrow

indicators.note: the close of a word is its final letter, so only the tail of 'shrubbery' is used

parts.note: the final letter

explanation.surface: A rough animal hole dug beside some bushes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to' reads as 'near'; it asks for the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Earthy humour is coarse and frank about bodily matters, which is crude in the vulgar sense.

clue.text: Hold that back about good editor given an honour

indicators.note: going back means reading the phrase for 'hold that' from right to left
one thing placed about another wraps around it, so the reversed word goes around 'good'

parts.note: to hold that something is true is to think it
G is the abbreviation for good
ed is the abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: A worthy newspaper editor receives a title.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hold that' is the verb phrase 'hold that X is true', i.e. think.
explanation.definitionFit: Being knighted means receiving a knighthood from the monarch, an honour carrying the title Sir.
